stage1.impression: Earth as the Death Star: a flat blue globe with a warm three-ring dish set high on the right and, in some variants, a tilted equatorial trench. The dish is the hero and it is well made: foreshortened along the right axis, its inner rings shifted toward the globe's centre so it reads as a bowl, warm against cool so it is still the first thing you see at 16 px. The rest is unresolved. The trench changes colour between variants (land green on the ocean-only spheres, a deeper blue on the land ones); on the land spheres it slices the continents like an orbit line, it is only about 4% of the diameter so it drops out below 32 px, and at dish 27 the dish almost sits on it (8 px gap on a 213 px globe, narrower than the 9 px trench). The continents are lumpy, emoji-grade shapes with crumbs: a blue lake nicking the dish's right rim in the Atlantic view, a sliver of Africa on the limb and a speck at the top right beside the dish in the Americas view. They mottle at 32 px. Everything is separated by hue, not value: land and sea are about 1.4:1 and red against green about 1:1, so in greyscale the Earth all but vanishes and, on land, the dish loses its rim. No one-colour version is shown. Where the dish lands matters: over north-east Africa and the Middle East (Africa view) it reads as a bullseye on a real region; over the Atlantic it reads as a dish. The disc-globe and two-tone directions lose the Earth and drown the dish. The ink versions hold. Best on the sheet: land, Americas, dish 24. Clever and legible at a glance, but not yet ownable: today it is the globe emoji with a sticker on it.

lead: Variant 8 (land, Americas, no trench, dish 24). It is the only land variant that is inside the fixed palette (4-6 draw the trench in #386C96, which is not one of the six colours). Its dish sits over open Atlantic water rather than on land, so the red surround is not laid on the equal-luminance green and the dish does not read as a target on a populated region. It shows two whole continents, the strongest Earth read on the sheet, and it has no trench to fight the land in one colour.
keep: The dish itself: three flat rings (surround 1.0, cone 0.70, dust cap 0.40) with the cone and cap shifted toward the globe's centre (DISH.depth 0.42). It reads as a concave divot and as a driver at once, and warm against the cool globe it stays the first read down to 16 px.

Dish 24 in the Death Star position (0.40, 0.36). It is the owner's 'slightly larger' divot without crowding the limb (about 18 px, 0.17 R, of globe between dish and edge on the sheet; dish 27 leaves 15 px). Over the Americas face it sits in open water, and the flat, stroke-free figure holds on ink as well as on paper (tile 11).

changes.problem: The dish is hemmed in on four sides: coasts touch or nearly touch its red surround, so the rim reads as crowded at full size, closes up at 32 px, and where red meets green the edge disappears in value and for red-green colour-blind viewers.
changes.evidence: sheet-1, tile 8 (land, Americas, no trench), measured on the 213 px globe: North America runs into the surround's upper left (0-1 px), South America's coast stops 3.6 px from the lower-left rim, the African coast 6.7 px from the right rim, and the piece at the top right 8 px from the top rim. Red #D2382F and green #4F7F3A are 1.02:1 in luminance; in a deuteranopia simulation of tile 7 (land, Africa, no trench) the surround merges into Africa.
changes.description: Keep all land at least 0.06 R (about 6 px on the 213 px sheet globe, 1 px at 32 px) from the dish's outer rim, in every variant. Cut back any coast that comes closer, along an arc concentric with the rim, and fill the cut with sea blue #4A90C8, so the red surround only ever touches blue. No new colour and no stroke.
changes.expected: A continuous band of sea blue rings the dish in the lead. Coasts that came near it (North America upper left, Africa right) end in a shallow arc 0.06 R short of the rim instead of grazing it. At 32 px the dish is a clean oval with blue all round.

accept.check: Does an unbroken band of sea blue separate the red surround from all land, all the way round the dish?

changes.problem: The card requires black-only and white-only versions and the sheet shows neither. As drawn, the figure would not survive one colour, because land, sea and surround are told apart by hue alone.
changes.evidence: sheet-1 has no one-colour tile. In a greyscale conversion of tiles 5-8 the continents nearly vanish (sea luminance 0.256 against land 0.171, 1.38:1), and the surround fuses with the land wherever they touch. Land running out to the limb (North America top left, Africa right in tile 8) would break the edge of a solid one-ink disc.
changes.description: Draw the lead in one ink with knock-outs only, no strokes. The disc is solid. Knock the continents out to the ground, but stop them 0.06 R inside the limb so the disc's edge stays a complete circle. Knock the dish out as the surround, with the cone solid (offset toward the centre as in colour) and the dust cap knocked out. Keep the 0.06 R collar from change 1 as solid ink between land and dish, and the surround's thin inner side at least 0.05 R wide. Show it black on paper #F2EFEA and white on ink #121114, each at 300, 64, 32 and 16 px.
changes.expected: Two new rows. The globe reads as Earth (light continents on a dark disc, or the reverse), the dish reads as a driver set into it, and the disc's outline is a complete circle. At 32 px North and South America and the dish's ring and cap are still distinct.

accept.check: Does the dish's knocked-out ring stand clear of every continent inside an unbroken black disc?

changes.problem: On the Americas face, Africa shows only as a thin crescent pressed against the right limb, and South America's north coast nearly touches the dish.
changes.evidence: sheet-1, tile 8 (land, Americas, no trench): the African piece is a 1,044 px² crescent only 17.8 px (0.17 R) deep from the limb and 6.7 px from the rim. South America is 3.6 px from the rim. At 32 px the crescent reads as a green fringe on the globe's edge.
changes.expected: The Earth turns 10 degrees under the fixed dish, which stays over open mid-Atlantic water (about 37 W, 32 N). South America drops clear below the dish (about 0.12 R, 13 px on the sheet globe). Africa becomes a solid bulge about 0.25 R deep on the right instead of a sliver. North America moves left and only grazes the dish, which the collar takes care of. Land outside the dish stays at about 28% of the disc (27% now).

accept.check: Is every piece of land on the right-hand edge at least about a fifth of the radius deep, with no crescent-thin sliver along the limb?

changes.problem: Islands and fragments turn into specks at small sizes and crowd the dish, which goes against the owner's 'minimal and polished'.
changes.evidence: sheet-1, tile 8: the southern tip of Greenland is a separate 356 px² piece (1.0% of the disc) 8 px off the dish's top rim; at 32 px it is a two-pixel speck beside the dish. Tile 7 has two more crumbs on the top limb (316 px² and 84 px²). Rotating the view does not remove the Greenland piece: it stays at 0.6-0.9% of the disc at every latitude from 4 to 14.
changes.description: After cutting the collar, delete any land piece smaller than 1.5% of the disc's area: about 530 px² on the 213 px sheet globe, roughly a blob 0.12 R across.
changes.expected: The lead carries only North America, South America and the bulge of Africa, with no island or speck anywhere on the disc.

accept.check: Is the land made only of large continental shapes, with no island, speck or stray fragment?

changes.problem: The coasts are lumpy rather than polished: stepped notches and thin hooks that break into speckle below 64 px.
changes.evidence: sheet-1, tile 8: notched east and Gulf coasts on North America and the thin Central American hook left of the dish. Tile 7: a stair-stepped West African coast. In a 32 px reduction these edges break into speckle.
changes.expected: The coasts read as a few long, smooth curves, and no notch, spit or hook narrower than about 0.1 R survives. The Gulf of Mexico and the bulge of Brazil still read.

accept.check: Is every coast a smooth curve with no notch, spit or hook narrower than about a tenth of the radius?

changes.problem: The figure is meant to kick like a speaker, but no motion is shown, so the driver idea and the way the brand moves cannot be judged.
changes.evidence: sheet-1 is a static sheet: it has no storyboard frames and no motion trace for the kick the card describes.
changes.description: A 1.0 s loop on the lead. From 0.00 to 0.06 s the cone and cap push out: DISH.depth goes from 0.42 to 0.12, so the inner rings swing toward concentric, and the dust cap scales from 1.00 to 1.06. From 0.06 to 0.30 s they spring back with one overshoot (depth 0.50 at 0.15 s) and rest at 0.42 by 0.30 s. From 0.04 s, one ring of sound leaves the rim: a flat red #D2382F band 0.05 R wide in the shape of the dish's rim, growing to 2.5 times the dish by 0.55 s, easing out and thinning to nothing as it passes the limb. From 0.55 to 1.00 s everything is still. The globe and the land never move.
changes.expected: A storyboard with one sharp push in the first frames and a single red ring that crosses the globe and leaves its edge by about 0.55 s. Then about half a second of stillness before the next beat: a kick, not a wobble.

changes.problem: Below 32 px the continents dissolve into speckle and only the dish survives.
changes.evidence: 16 px reductions of tiles 5-8: the green and blue boundaries go below a pixel, the disc reads as mottled, and only the dish is still legible.
changes.description: A small-size cut for 24 px and below: the disc and the dish only, with no land. The dish keeps the same position, size and rings. In colour the disc is blue #4A90C8; in one ink it is a solid disc with the surround and cap knocked out and the cone solid. Show it at 24 and 16 px beside the full figure at 32 px.
changes.expected: At 16 px the mark is a clean blue disc with one warm dish at the upper right and no green specks, and it is plainly the same figure as the full version at 32 px.

accept.check: Does the 16 px version show a clean disc with a single warm dish at the upper right and no specks of land?

most_important: Make variant 8 the lead and keep all land 0.06 R clear of the dish (change 1). That one rule removes the four near-tangencies around the rim and keeps the red surround off the green it cannot be told from in value. It is also what makes a one-colour version possible: without it the knocked-out surround runs into the knocked-out continents.
out_of_scope: The fixed palette puts land and sea only 1.38:1 apart in luminance, and the red surround 1.02:1 against the green, so the Earth reads by hue alone (weak in greyscale and for red-green colour-blind viewers). A darker green or lighter blue would fix this at the source, but the palette is fixed; the collar and the one-colour drawing work around it.
The deeper blue #386C96 used for the trench on variants 4-6 is not in the fixed palette. Any trench that comes back must be drawn in one of the six fixed colours.
for_owner: Trench or no trench. We lead without it: the divot alone carries the Death Star, and on the land views the trench slices the continents, is under 1.5 px wide at 32 px and needs an off-palette blue. If you want it back, we would bring it back in violet #6C4BA3 (the darkest fixed colour, 1.9:1 against the sea) at TRENCH.half 0.06; in one colour it would be a knocked-out line.

Confirm what 'more earth on the outside' means. We read it as continents on the sphere, and we also keep the dish at 24 rather than 27 so more globe shows around it (27 leaves less globe at the limb and covers more land). The lead does both.

Whether the speaker figure should borrow from the main six-disc globe (variants 9-10). We recommend not: cut into the disc globe, the dish loses its place and the main mark is spoiled. The two figures should stay distinct.
Whether the figure drops its continents at 24 px and below (change 7). This is a system rule, and you may prefer the land at every size even if it turns to speckle.

Which face of the Earth is shown. We advise keeping the Americas face for all uses: turning to Africa or Europe puts the dish on land, where the red-orange-yellow rings read as a target on a populated region.
